passage: Each species of fig tree is pollinated by its own species of tiny wasp, which can complete its life cycle only inside that fig's enclosed flowers; the wasp pollinates the fig as it lays its eggs, and neither partner reproduces without the other. Because adult wasps live only a day or two, a wasp emerging from a ripe fig must find another tree of the same species already in flower, and fig trees in a given forest tend to flower at staggered times rather than all at once. Ecologists who model this system note that a fig population too sparse or too synchronized in its flowering would leave emerging wasps with nowhere to go. Their analysis implies that the long-term survival of a fig species in a forest ______
question: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.text: depends only on the total number of fig trees present, regardless of when those particular trees happen to come into flower.
is unaffected by the short lifespan of the pollinating wasps, since the trees can be pollinated by the wind whenever no wasp arrives.
would be substantially improved if all the fig trees in the forest happened to come into flower at exactly the same time rather than at staggered intervals.
requires both a sufficient density of trees and a spread of flowering times that lets short-lived wasps always find a receptive tree.

explanation: The correct answer is D. The model says a population that is too sparse or too synchronized strands the short-lived wasps, so survival needs enough trees and a staggering of bloom times. D names both conditions. A drops the timing, which the passage shows is essential. B contradicts the premise that the fig depends entirely on its wasp, not on wind. C gets the timing backward: simultaneous flowering would leave wasps emerging from late figs with no receptive tree to reach.
